India_Insight: Ola, Uber, Rapido, Namma Yatri compete aggressively on price. Zero-switching-cost for riders. Driver poaching common. Low differentiation except network density.
Pricing_Implication: Any visible price increase risks immediate rider/driver loss. Zone-based caps less visible than uniform caps.
Switching_Behavior: Riders: multi-apping is norm (75%+ have 2+ apps). Switching cost = zero. Drivers: multi-platform driving standard. Switch triggered by 5-10% price differential.
Defensibility: LOW: Price comparison takes <10 seconds. Only defense is network density (wait time) and loyalty lock-in.

India_Insight: Price-sensitive market. Multi-apping is standard. Auto-rickshaws, metro, buses as cheap substitutes. Low brand loyalty outside premium segment.
Pricing_Implication: Surge above 1.5x triggers app-switching. Satisfaction cliff at 1.5x confirms. Loyalty protection mitigates for high-value riders.
Switching_Behavior: Frequent riders: least price-sensitive (LTV/CAC 1.47), some brand affinity. Occasional: moderate sensitivity. Rare: highest churn risk, switch on any surge >1.25x.
Defensibility: MODERATE for frequent segment (habit + convenience). LOW for occasional/rare (pure price comparison). Loyalty programs increase switching costs.

India_Insight: Driver supply elastic in medium term. Multi-platform driving common. Strike risk if earnings drop. Regulatory pressure on driver welfare.
Pricing_Implication: Capping surge reduces driver earnings on high-demand trips. Must balance driver retention with rider pricing.
Switching_Behavior: Drivers switch platforms based on earnings per hour + incentive bonuses. Surge caps reduce driver motivation during peak. Strike risk if >15% earnings cut.
Defensibility: MODERATE: Driver supply elastic but platform with highest utilization retains more. Zone caps preserve driver earnings on commercial/transit (high-demand).

India_Insight: Auto-rickshaws (negotiable fare), public transit (Delhi Metro, Mumbai Local), two-wheelers, walking for short trips. Substitute cost often below ride-hail base fare.
Pricing_Implication: Short-trip negative margins reflect substitute competition. Zone caps on residential (short trips) limit price sensitivity damage.
Switching_Behavior: Residential zones: high substitute availability (walking, auto, metro). Commercial: moderate (time pressure > price). Transit hubs: low substitute salience (need last-mile).
Defensibility: LOW for short trips <3km (auto/walking cheaper). MODERATE for 3-10km (convenience factor). HIGH for >10km (few viable substitutes). Zone caps on residential acknowledge this.

India_Insight: Low capital entry (open-source dispatch like Namma Yatri). Network effects create moat. Regulatory licensing is barrier. But local players can enter specific cities/zones.
Pricing_Implication: Zone-based governance easier to defend than uniform pricing - adapts to local competitive dynamics.
Switching_Behavior: New entrants target price-sensitive riders with zero-surge or flat-fare. Namma Yatri model (zero commission) attracts drivers. Entry easiest in single-city niches.
Defensibility: MODERATE: Network density is real moat. Zone governance adapts to local conditions. But zero-commission models can undercut on price. Must match on driver earnings.
